newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn wants to maintain aid to east Germany.
newsitem.headline: Bonn wants to maintain aid to east Germany.

text.p: The German government aims to maintain investment incentives to ex-communist east Germany at current levels, but stopped short of giving the plan its final approval, a spokesman said on Tuesday.

A new plan by Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt would allocate 5.7 billion marks ($3.3 billion) in investment bonuses annually to the region for six years from 1999, and create an extra 2,800 training places there, spokesman Peter Hausmann said.
The plan would eliminate 11 billion marks annually in special depreciation allowances for the east, but it would have a similar economic impact at lower cost to the government, Hausmann said.
"This would keep payments at current levels and help to boost training opportunities there," Hausmann told a routine government news conference.

The conservative state of Bavaria, ruled by Finance Minister Theo Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU), has been pressuring Bonn to review the plan in detail, given the severe budget constraints it faces.

Since unification in 1990, over one trillion marks in aid has been transferred to the region, generating friction between east and west. The aid has been partly financed by the solidarity tax surcharge, which Bonn has promised to cut next year to 5.5 percent from 7.5 percent.

Average unemployment in east Germany is about 17 percent, compared with about 10 percent in the west, but in some places it is as high as 25 percent. Politicians say the gap between the affluent west and poorer east will widen without continued financial injections from Bonn.

Hausmann said Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet had approved Rexrodt's plan in principle, but it would need support from regional leaders in east Germany before Bonn could give the plan its final stamp of approval.
Plans to cut the solidarity surcharge have met with stiff resistance from regional leaders in east Germany but praise from western leaders, who complain their states bear the brunt of the cost.
Waigel dismissed suspicions he had tried to stop Rexrodt's plan from going ahead because of concerns about Germany's widening budget deficit, saying one had nothing to do with the other.
Some west German parliamentarians have joined the eastern leaders in their support for plans to maintain the vast cash injections for fear already depressed areas could get worse.

"No one in west Germany will be happy in future if poor-house conditions prevail in some regions in east Germany," Friedhelm Ost, chairman Bonn's parliamentary committee for economic affairs, told InfoRadio in Berlin.

"We are also obliged by the constitution to create roughly equal working, economic and living conditions. That's why I do not think much of the exaggerated regional egotism you have here in western Germany," Ost said.

Rexrodt's plan would double investment bonuses to 10 percent from five percent for larger enterprises, and to 20 percent from 10 percent for small and medium-sized enterprises, concentrated in manufacturing and related services. ($ = 1.705 German Marks)
